title: The Licence Ceiling: Why a Trade Business Stops Growing at the Owner's Calendar
linkedin:
Tradies National Health Month is rightly focused on the toll of always being on the tools. There is a commercial pattern sitting underneath that toll worth naming.

In a lot of licensed trade businesses, electricians, plumbers, HVAC and refrigeration specialists among them, one person holds almost everything of value: the quoting judgement, the supplier relationships, the licence itself.

Revenue can look solid for years without anyone testing what happens the day that person is off the tools.

That test tends to show up one of two ways. An owner tries to add a second crew and finds margin does not lift the way they expected, because a new hire needs months of supervision before their quoting and quality match the owners. Or an owner has a conversation about selling, and a buyer discounts the price heavily because the business stops the day the owner does.

We see this most clearly in the numbers behind a second van. The wages, ute finance, tools and insurance land on day one. The extra revenue usually takes two quarters or more to catch up, because a new hire needs real supervision before their work carries the same quality and speed as the owners. A lot of owners read that early dip as proof the expansion does not work, when the real issue is that the transition period was never costed properly to begin with.

Neither problem gets solved by working harder. Both get solved by deliberately building a second and third person who can quote and run a job to the same standard, well before growth or a sale forces the issue.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

facebook:
Genuine question for anyone running a trade business, sparky, plumber, HVAC, refrigeration: if you took a fortnight off tomorrow, would the quoting and the quality stay the same without you?

That is the pattern we keep seeing. The business runs well, but almost everything valuable, the pricing judgement, the supplier relationships, the licence, lives in one person's head. It does not show up as a problem until someone tries to add a second crew, or until a buyer starts asking questions.

Worth thinking about before either of those moments arrives, not during.

A note for trade business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria as Tradies National Health Month continues through August. Most of the conversation this month rightly focuses on the physical and mental toll of the work, the early starts, the isolation, always being on call. There is a commercial pattern sitting underneath that toll that is worth a closer look.

In many licensed trade businesses, electricians, plumbers, HVAC and refrigeration specialists among them, one person carries almost everything of value: the quoting judgement, the relationships with good suppliers, and the licence the business trades under. Revenue can look healthy for years without anyone testing what happens on the day that person steps back.

That test tends to arrive when an owner tries to add a second crew and finds profit does not lift the way expected, or when a sale conversation starts and a buyer prices in a heavy discount for a business that cannot run without its owner. Both situations trace back to the same structural gap, and both are far easier to fix while there is no pressure to fix them quickly.
